order_excerpt: IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY WELLINGTON I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI TE WHANGANUI-A-TARA ROHE [2025] NZERA 713 3349980 BETWEEN CAMERON WONG Applicant AND OBERS BROTHERS CONSTRUCTION LIMITED in liquidation Respondent Member of Authority: Geoff O’Sullivan Representatives: Hayley Johnson, advocate for the Applicant No appearance for the Respondent Investigation Meeting: By audiovisual link on 8 July 2025 Submissions and other 6 November 2025 information Received: Determination: 07 November 2025 DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY Employment Relationship Problem After the Investigation Meeting had occurred the respondent company was placed in liquidation. This prevented the issuing of this determination. However, on 6 November 2025 the Authority was advised the Liquidator had given permission for the matter to proceed. Mr Wong is a painter and says he was employed by Obers Brothers Construction Limited (Obers) for just over eleven months. He has been in the painting industry for some 17 years. He says despite asking for it, Obers failed to provide Mr Wong with a written employment agreement. Mr Wong says that on 5 August 2024 Jason Obers confronted him at work about a comment he had allegedly made to a builder suggesting that non-painters shouldn’t handle painting tasks. Mr Wong says he was told to: “Leave, pack your belongings, I’ll pay you out, and I have other painters ready to start tomorrow”. Mr Wong says he felt extremely intimidated and started to pack his work tools into his van but before leaving the work site, approached Jason Obers asking if he would accept him providing notice to end his employment. Mr Wong says he did this because he believed he needed to do so in order to have his notice period paid out. He says that Jason Obers replied again: “Just get your fucking shit and fuck off”. On 7 August 2024, Mr Wong received his final pay which was for 38 hours only. He says he received no holiday pay or payment in lieu of notice. Because he believed he needed to do so, on 8 August 2024, Mr Wong submitted an official resignation letter, along with a medical certificate stating he was unfit for work. He says he did this because he had not received any advice on the matter and thought if he did not do this he may not get his entitlements. On 14 August 2024 he received a further payslip. Annual leave was shown to be 153 hours accrued, but his pay was shown as zero. To date, he has not received his final wages, annual holiday leave entitlement, outstanding holiday pay, or notice. Discussion and analysis Obers did not attend the investigation meeting, nor did it engage in the Authority’s investigation. It was clear, however, from the Authority’s file that Obers was aware of the proceedings. Because there was no attendance at the investigation meeting, it raised a question of whether or not I should proceed in its absence. For this reason, the commencement of the investigation meeting was adjourned for 15 minutes in case Obers or any of their witnesses were running late. No one appeared and accordingly I decided to proceed on the basis that as Obers was aware the investigation meeting was being held, was aware of the date and time of the investigation. All the witnesses who gave evidence before the Authority affirmed their evidence on affirmation. Mr Wong claims he was dismissed from his employment unjustifiably. He started to look for new work almost immediately and it did not take him long to secure new work contracts. They did, however, involve a lot of travel. He says the impact on him from an emotional perspective was significant. It has affected his relationship with his family which include Jason Obers’ parents, his aunty and uncle, his own father and his nana. He says it affected his confidence and he feels like he was completely used. Mr Wong’s mother, Mary Birch, also gave evidence about the impact the dismissal had on her son. She said she supported him after the dismissal and directly observed the hurt and humiliation he suffered as a result of it. Sean Stuart-Red also gave evidence in support of Mr Wong, who he described as a friend and colleague. He also recalled Mr Wong being sworn at and told to leave. As Obers was not there to justify or speak to its actions, it follows that I find Mr Wong’s dismissal unjustified. Accordingly, he is entitled to a consideration of remedies. Mr Wong claims $8,155.00 gross in unpaid holiday entitlements. He has calculated this on his hourly rate of $35.00 an hour for the eleven months he was employed. This gives a total of 153 hours of leave equalling $5,355.00. To this he has added an additional 80 hours for a two week notice period. He also claims $12,242.00 in lost wages. He bases this on the fact he was earning approximately $1,400.00 gross per week and in the 13 weeks post dismissal he invoiced approximately $5,958.00 for labour. This equates to a loss of $12,242.00 in gross. Mr Wong also claims damages for hurt, humiliation, injury to feelings and loss of dignity of $30,000.00. Penalties were not pursued to the extent no evidence was offered in support of them. In respect of lost wages, unpaid wages, unpaid notice and holiday pay, I accept Mr Wong’s evidence. Although the evidence of the emotional effect the dismissal had on Mr Wong was compelling, I consider an appropriate award is $17,500.00. Summary of orders Obers Brothers Construction Limited has unjustifiably dismissed Cameron Wong. It is ordered to pay him the following: (a) Unpaid holiday entitlements of $5,355.00; (b) Two weeks’ notice totalling $2,800.00; (c) Lost wages of $12,242.00; (d) Damages for the humiliation, injury to feelings and loss of dignity of $17,500.00. The above payments are to be made within 28 days from the date of this determination. Costs Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, Cameron Wong may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum Obers Brothers Construction Limited will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [49] Accordingly, Hongyu must pay Mr Liu the further amount of $1,937.44 due to him as arrears of holiday pay. Order for payment of interest on arrears [50] Mr Liu had been entitled to have the use of the wages and holiday pay due to him from the date his employment ended. He was denied the benefit and use of that money from then. Accordingly it was also appropriate to order interest be paid on the arrears now confirmed as due to him from that date. [51] Hongyu must pay Mr Liu interest on those amounts (totalling $7,377.44) from 24 June 2024 until those arrears are paid in full. This order is made under clause 11 of Schedule 2 of the ER Act. Interest is to be calculated by using the Civil debt interest calculator.3 Breaches of employment standards [52] The ER Act identifies certain provisions of the ER Act, the HA and WPA as “employment standards”. Under s 142Y and s 142W of the ER Act a person in a position of responsibility with an employer may be identified as “involved” in breaches of those standards. The Authority may then give leave to an employee who is owed arrears by that employer to recover those arrears from the involved person if the employing company or organisation is not able to pay the arrears. [53] Legend and Hongyu breached those standards in the following way: (i) Legend and Hongyu failed to provide a copy of Mr Liu’s written employment agreement when requested by Mr Liu’s advocate. This was a breach of s 64(3) of the ER Act. Mr Liu’s evidence was that he had signed a written employment agreement when he began work for Legend but did not have a copy. There was no written employment agreement for his employment with Hongyu. (ii) Hongyu failed to pay the wages comprising Mr Liu’s notice at the end of his employment. This was a breach of WPA s 4. (iii) Hongyu failed to pay all of Mr Liu’s annual leave entitlements at the end of his employment. This was a breach of HA s 24 and s 25. (iv) Hongyu and Legend failed to provide immediate access to wage and time records for Mr Liu when requested by his advocate. This was a breach of ER Act s 130(2). Mr Wang a person involved in breach of employment standards [54] There was no dispute that Mr Wang was knowingly concerned in each of those breaches in his role as a director of Legend and as manager of the HY Kitchen business. 3 www.justice.govt.nz/fines/civil-debt-interest-calculator. Throughout Mr Wang, as he accepted in his evidence, was the person responsible for making all relevant decisions about what was done or not done in respect of Mr Liu’s employment and payments to him. Mr Wang, as apparent from his evidence, had access to advice from the company’s external accountant and, later, a lawyer but he was the person in the position of carrying out the management of both the Legend and Hongyu companies.4 His text messages to Mr Liu in June, July and August 2024 confirmed he was, as defined by s 142W of the ER Act, a person involved in making and communicating decisions about all the matters that comprised breaches of the employment standards by Legend and Hongyu. Leave to pursue Mr Wang for unpaid arrears [55] Accordingly, leave is granted to Mr Liu to seek recover from Mr Wang any arrears of wages and holiday pay owed to him if Hongyu is unable to pay those amounts. Penalties [56] Mr Liu sought orders for penalties against Legend and Hongyu. This was mostly in respect of the same breaches of statutory provisions that comprised the breaches of employment standards. ER Act s 65 – failure to provide a written employment agreement [57] Mr Liu’s statement of problem did not seek a penalty under s 64(3) over Legend not providing him with a requested copy of his written employment agreement with that company. He did seek a penalty under s 65 of the ER Act for failure to provide him with an employment agreement at all. This, on his own evidence, related only to Hongyu. There was no evidence or explanation for why Hongyu had not done so. [58] Weighing the relevant factors for determining an appropriate penalty for that breach under s 133A of the ER Act, and the range of penalties awarded in similar circumstances, Hongyu must pay a penalty of $2,000 for its breach of s 65 of the Act. WPA s 4 – failure to pay wages when due [59] Mr Wang accepted Hongyu should have paid Mr Liu four weeks’ wages as notice at the time of terminating his employment at the end of June 2024. Its failure to do so was a breach of its obligations under s 4 of the WPA to pay the entire amount of 4 Employment Relations Act 2000 s 142W(1) and (3). wages due to a worker without deduction. This breach denied Mr Liu money he was entitled to have the use of from the end of his employment and caused him hardship in meeting his household’s financial commitments. Hongyu was liable to a penalty for that breach. [60] Weighing the relevant factors under s 133A of the ER Act and the range of penalties awarded in similar circumstances, Hongyu must pay a penalty of $2,000 for its breach of s 4 of the WPA. HA s 24 and s 25 – failure to pay full annual leave entitlements at end of employment [61] The shortfall in payment of Mr Liu’s annual leave entitlements was a breach of the HA provisions requiring complete payment of those entitlements for the full year he had worked for Legend and the part year he worked for Hongyu. This breach denied Mr Liu use of money he was entitled to have the from the end of his employment and caused him hardship in meeting his household’s financial commitments. Hongyu had ‘inherited’ the liability for his annual leave entitlements with Legend so is liable for the penalty. [62] Weighing the relevant factors under s 133A of the ER Act and the range of penalties awarded in similar circumstances, Hongyu must pay a penalty of $2,000 for its breach of s 24 and s 25 of the HA. ERA s 130(2) – failure to provide wage and time records [63] By letter of 10 September 2024 Mr Liu’s advocate asked for a copy of the wage and time records for Mr Liu’s employment with Legend and Hongyu. His letter drew the companies’ attention to the statutory obligation to provide immediate access in response to such a request and the risk of a penalty if they failed to do so. [64] Neither company provided the requested records. This resulted in Mr Liu’s claims having to be assessed from information available in his bank statements, IRD records and some pay slips. It hampered the straightforward presentation and assessment of his claim. Legend and Hongyu are each liable to a penalty for the breach. [65] Weighing the relevant factors under s 133A of the ER Act and the range of penalties awarded in similar circumstances, Hongyu and Legend must each pay a penalty of $1,000 for their respective breaches of s 130(2) of the ERA Act. Proportional outcome [66] As a crosscheck, the total penalties awarded (totalling $8,000 against the two respondent companies) was not disproportionate to the nature of the breaches, affecting the whole of the employment relationship, and the amount of arrears awarded.5 Penalties to be paid to the Crown [67] Mr Liu sought an order for part of any penalties imposed to be paid to him. The remedies awarded to him by orders made elsewhere in this determination address the wrong done to him. Penalties are not a means to obtain additional compensation for the various failures of Legend and Hongyu to meet their statutory obligations. Rather, the full amount of the penalties imposed on Legend and Hongyu are to be paid to the Crown. This recognises two aspects of the public interest in matters of this type. Firstly, there is the overarching public interest in maintaining employment standards for workers. Secondly, there is a public interest in protecting businesses who do comply with those standards from the unfair competitive advantage gained by businesses who reduce their costs of operation through failing or avoiding their obligations to meet the statutory standards regarding pay and other entitlements. This relates specifically to the object of the ER Act at s 3(ab) to promote effective enforcement of employment standards through the Labour Inspectorate and the Authority. Summary and orders Personal grievance [68] Mr Liu was unjustifiably dismissed by Hongyu. For his unjustified dismissal Hongyu must pay Mr Liu the following sums within 28 days of the date of this determination: (i) $5,440 as wages lost as a result of the grievance; and (ii) $15,000 as compensation for the humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings. 5 Rural Practice Limited v A Labour Inspector [2025] NZEmpC 198, at [56] – [58]. Arrears [69] Mr Liu is also entitled to arrears of wages comprising $5,440 as wages for a four week notice period and $1,937.44 for outstanding annual leave entitlements. Interest on those amounts is to be paid for the period from 24 June 2024 until the arrears are paid in full. The arrears, with interest, must be paid by Hongyu to Mr Liu within 28 days of the date of this determination. Breach of employment standards [70] Both Legend and Hongyu breached employment standards in their employment relationships with Mr Liu. Legend failed to provide a copy of a written employment agreement when requested and had not provided immediate access to requested time and wage records. Hongyu failed to pay wages when due by not paying a notice period at the end of its employment of Mr Liu, failed to pay full annual leave entitlements at the end of the employment, and did not provide immediate access to requested time and wage records. [71] Mr Wang was a person involved in those breaches of employment standards. Under s 142Y of the Act Mr Liu is granted leave to recover the arrears of wages and holiday pay due to him to the extent Hongyu is unable to pay those amounts. Penalties [72] For their respective breach of employment standards and other statutory provisions, Hongyu and Legend must pay the following penalties to the Authority for transfer to a Crown account within 28 days of the date of this determination: (i) From Hongyu $2,000 for its breach of s 65 of the ER Act; $2,000 for its breach of s 4 of the WPA; $2,000 for its breach of s 24 and s 25 of the HA; and $1,000 for its breach of s 130(2) of the ER Act. (ii) From Legend a penalty of $1,000 for its breach of s 130(2) of the ER Act. Costs [73] Mr Liu is also entitled to an award of costs and expenses for successfully bringing his application to the Authority. The investigation meeting was held over two separate days but, taken together, did not take a whole day so a portion of the Authority’s usual daily tariff of $4,500 is appropriately applied to setting the contribution which the respondents must pay towards his costs of representation in this case. Accordingly, costs are awarded on the basis of two-thirds of the daily tariff, that is $3,000. [74] The respondents must also reimburse Mr Liu for the fee of $71.55 paid to lodge his application in the Authority. [75] The respondents are jointly and severally liable for those costs and expenses which must also be paid within 28 days of the date of this determination. Robin Arthur Member of the Employment Relations Authority

order_excerpt: determination IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY AUCKLAND I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI TᾹMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE [2025] NZERA 694 3347760 3368865 3382143 BETWEEN IGD Applicant in 3347760 Respondent in 3368865 & 3382143 AND SAJ Respondent in 3347760 Applicant in 3368865 & 3382143 Member of Authority: Nicola Craig Representatives: Stephen Corlett, counsel for IGD Donna Pokere-Phillips, advocate for SAJ Investigation Meeting: On the papers Submissions received: 29 October 2025 from IGD 29 and 30 October 2025 from SAJ Determination: 30 October 2025 THIRD DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY Employment relationship problem [1] SAJ is Te Tumu Whakarae, chief executive of IGD, a charitable organisation providing community services. Both are identified by randomly chosen letters. [2] There are three Authority matters between the parties which have resulted so far in three determinations, including this one. In the first matter IGD sought orders and an interim order was granted restraining SAJ from publishing the content of certain material from mediation, along with a non-publication order.1 In the second matter SAJ sought to be reinstated from suspension by IGD as part of an investigative/disciplinary process, along with other orders. The orders sought were not granted.2 [3] Then SAJ lodged an application about “contractual and governance breaches” along with unjustified disadvantage harming SAJ.3 The parties agreed that all three matters should be heard together. An investigation meeting was held in September 2025 regarding the three matters with submissions subsequently received. Submissions regarding one further issue about contractual arrangements were still being received up until yesterday. The Authority’s process [4] On 29 October 2025 SAJ’s representative filed a memorandum which included seeking orders regarding disciplinary action. Given that SAJ had until the following day (30 October 2025) to provide any response to the letter on behalf of IGD, any reply submissions were urgently sought from IGD and provided on 29 October 2025. A reply submission was then filed on SAJ’s behalf today, which focuses on tikanga Māori. No affidavit evidence has been supplied supporting material in that submission. Given the time pressures, this determination will be issued but a supporting affidavit will be filed as soon as practicable. [5] As permitted by s 174E of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) this determination has not recorded everything received from the parties but has stated findings, expressed conclusions and specified orders made as a result. Non-publication order [6] An interim non-publication order is in place regarding the parties’ names and any identifying details in relation to these three proceedings between the parties. The involvement of substantial numbers of people at investigation meeting days as well as the nature of the IGD organisation and its connections will need to be considered in deciding whether a permanent order should be made. 1 IGD v SAJ [2024] NZERA 777 (file 3347760). 2 SAJ v IGD [2025] NZERA 397 (file 3382143). 3 File 3382143. [7] In the meantime the reply submissions received today refer to a tikanga Māori need to respond to an iwi request for a briefing hui next week with SAJ. It is not evident whether a similar request has been made to IGD. No specific request regarding the non-publication order is made on SAJ’s behalf although it is clear an obligation to attend the hui is felt. [8] Given the need to deal with the order sought by SAJ before any disciplinary action is taken, I make no immediate decision on non-publication, with the order remaining in place. The parties are encouraged to reach an agreed position on whether and to what extent the interim order should be amended. They should revert to the Authority, which would then be amenable to assessing the non-publication order. The issue [9] The issue for determination is whether an interim order should be made regarding the disciplinary action by IGD against SAJ. Events [10] For the sake of completeness I summarise SAJ’s issues which were identified to be investigated at the recent investigation meeting – did IGD breach its contractual obligation to pay SAJ a bonus entitlement, act in an unjustifiable manner causing her disadvantage (including a pattern of undermining, harassment and cultural disregard) or unjustifiably suspend her, along with what remedies should be ordered? [11] It was evident at the recent investigation meeting that IGD was proceeding with its investigation into SAJ and had not undertaken to stop that investigation or any disciplinary action until after a substantive determination was issued regarding the three proceedings. [12] By way of a lengthy 23 October 2025 emailed letter IGD wrote to SAJ. It set out its summary of the allegations made regarding SAJ, SAJ’s views/discussion and its “preliminary findings” on those allegations. It concludes there has been misconduct and serious misconduct and the organisation is considering terminating SAJ’s employment. SAJ is given the opportunity to provide any response by close of business on 30 October 2025. Submissions [13] Submissions for SAJ argue that IGD’s letter amounts to a further breach of natural justice and risks “undermining the integrity of the Authority’s process on matters already before it”. [14] Reference is made to a request on SAJ’s behalf to IGD to defer any disciplinary decision until after the Authority’s determination, which was declined. [15] Today’s submissions on IGD’s behalf refer to tikanga Māori forming a part of New Zealand’s common law.4 It is argued that a call yesterday from an iwi leader and reference to mention of SAJ/IGD at a high-level forum (despite SAJ not speaking to anyone about the case) takes this case in a different direction to others where Authority intervention was not seen as warranted. Reference is made to the leader referring to the IGD organisation as a taonga of the iwi. [16] Submissions for IGD oppose the order sought by SAJ and rely on cases declining to make interim orders preventing any decision to dismiss.5 The issues awaiting substantive determination are summarised as whether a performance appraisal was a fabrication, the bonus claim, allegations of breaches of confidentiality by discussing employment matters with others and unfair micromanagement. It is submitted that these issues would not be pre-empted by IGD concluding its disciplinary process, regardless of whether action is taken against SAJ. [17] IGD is concerned that it has already delayed progression of the investigation to accommodate the current proceedings. An order as sought by SAJ would delay that process further. The organisation identifies disadvantages to it in continuing to have to pay SAJ as well as its Interim/Acting CEO, being unable to look to appointing a permanent CEO (if dismissal occurs) or reintegrating SAJ (if not) and staff facing continued uncertainty. Conclusions [18] No finding is made regarding whether IGD’s recent letter amounts to a breach of natural justice or is otherwise an unjustifiable action by IGD. 4 Relying on Takamore v Clarke [2012] NZSC 5 Ports of Auckland Ltd v Findlay [2017] NZEmpC 45 and Moke v Raukura Hauora o Tainui Trust [2023] NZERA 603. [19] There are considerations which speak against intervening in IGD’s process. [20] In the Authority’s second determination it was noted to be unusual for the Authority to intervene to restrain an employer from taking further steps in an employer’s investigation or disciplinary process based on the Employment Court’s rationale in Ports of Auckland Ltd v Findlay: … [O]rders restraining an employer from proceeding with an investigative/disciplinary process into concerns about employee conduct will be rare. That will be even more so where, as here, permanent orders are sought restraining an employer from taking any further steps at all, effectively halting the employer’s processes in their tracks. The reasons for this are clear. The first point is that such an approach runs the risk of putting the cart before the horse, and pre-judging the endpoint that an employer might (but might not) get to. It also runs the risk of cutting across an employer’s obligation to investigate concerns, including health and safety concerns impacting on other employees. Also relevant is the interest, both to the individuals concerned, and more generally, in allowing such processes to run their course without undue interruption and delay. A stop-start approach to an investigative and disciplinary process which invites intervention along the way from the Authority; the Employment Court on challenge; and potentially the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court by way of further appeal; is plainly undesirable for public policy reasons.6 [21] In the second determination it was concluded: The compelling undesirability of interrupting an employer’s process is referred to above. I am not persuaded that this is one of those very rare situations where an order halting an investigatory/disciplinary process should be made.7 [22] As the substantive issues awaiting determination are very largely independent of the issues in the disciplinary process, SAJ’s substantive issues would not be pre- empted by IGD progressing with its disciplinary process. Rather SAJ could pursue an additional personal grievance claim if not satisfied with the disciplinary process or outcome. [23] However, the involvement of the iwi leader and tikanga obligations do involve different considerations. I consider that there is a basis to see this as a very rare case where a brief halting of the employer’s process is warranted to allow the hui to proceed. As IGD points out it has been a fairly lengthy period since it started its process but a short halt will likely cause little additional detriment to it. 6 Ports of Auckland Ltd v Findlay [2017] NZEmpC 45 at [23]. 7 Above at n 2, at [108]. [24] I order that IGD is to take no further steps in its disciplinary process regarding SAJ until 9am on Monday 10 November 2025. Costs [25] Costs are reserved. Nicola Craig Member of the Employment Relations Authority

order_excerpt: Remedies Personal Grievance [46] As Mr Isaako has been successful with his unjustified dismissal claim I must turn to consider what remedies he may be entitled to. I may award any of the remedies provided for under s 123 of the Act. Reimbursement of lost wages [47] Mr Isaako seeks reimbursement of 3 months in lost wages for the earnings he has lost as a result of his unjustified dismissal pursuant to s 123(1)(b) of the Act. [48] Where the Authority finds that an employee has a personal grievance, and that the employee has lost remuneration as a result of the personal grievance, the Authority must order the employer to pay to the employee the lesser of a sum equal to that lost remuneration or to 3 months’ ordinary time remuneration. [49] Mr Isaako was summarily dismissed without notice. Mr Isaako is entitled to be paid his hourly rate at 39 hours per week for the 13 weeks after his employment ended. 9 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 103A. [50] Mr Isaako is entitled to $15,210.00 (gross) in lost wages pursuant to s123(1)(b) ERA of the Act. Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings [51] Mr Isaako gave evidence about ABS’s decision to dismiss him and the process leading up to that decision. Mr Isaako stated that the abruptness of the termination caused significant distress to both him and his whanau, particularly as he had to support his whanau who relied on his income from ABS to meet their financial obligations. His family has missed out on a lot of family meetings, outings and interactive activities with his family due to his financial circumstances [52] He said he found it hard to get over how he had been treated He said he had withdrawn from social interactions and had struggled with his confidence. He had avoided meeting friends and family because of the shame and pressure of unemployment. [53] I determine that an appropriate award to compensate for the effects on him, accepting his evidence, was $15,000.00. ABS is ordered to pay to Mr Isaako compensation of $15,000.00. Contribution [54] Under the Act I am required to consider if remedies should be reduced for blameworthy conduct by Mr Isaako that contributed to the situation giving rise to his grievance.10 Mr Isaako was unjustifiably dismissed and did not contribute to his dismissal, and warrants no reduction in remedy. Wage arrears- holiday pay [55] ABS failed to pay Mr Isaako public holiday pay, and annual leave entitlements. Further ABS failed to provide accurate wage and time records; however I accept Mr Isaako’s calculation for what is owed. 10 Employment Relations Act , s 124. Public Holidays [56] Mr Isaako is entitled to payment of five public holidays (Waitangi Day, Easter Friday, Easter Sunday, Anzac Day, Kings Birthday) at 8.5 hours per day, being $1,275.00 (gross). Annual Holidays [57] ABS is to pay Mr Isaako’s annual holiday pay of 8 percent for his period of employment of 18 weeks.(18 x $1,170.00 per week =$21,060 x 8% =$1,684.80). [58] ABS is to pay Mr Isaako’s $1,684.80 (gross) annual holiday. No penalty in relation to ABS’s breaches of the Holidays Act 2003, Wages Protection Act 1983 and Employment Relations Act 2000. [59] The application for penalties is in relation to ABS’s breaches of the Holidays Act 2003 and Wages Protection Act 1983 are statutorily barred, as they were not raised until the lodging of Mr Isaako’s closing submissions on 26 August 2025, outside the 12-month time limit.11 [60] In regard to failure to provide wages and time records, I do not find in the circumstances of this case that the breach is sufficiently serious to warrant a penalty to be imposed under s 130 of the Act. The Authority orders against ABS to pay arrears to Mr Isaako was sufficient enough to address Mr Isaako’s claim. Accordingly, no penalty order is made against ABS. Summary of orders [61] ABS Builders Limited is ordered, within 28 days of the date of this determination, to make payment to Lautusi Isaako; (a) $15,210.00 (gross) as reimbursement of lost wages of 3 months’ salary; and12 (b) $15,000.00 as compensation for hurt humiliation and injury to feelings;13 and (c) $1,684.80 (gross) for annual holiday pay; and 11 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 135(5),Wages protection Act1983, s13(1), Holidays Act 2003, s75 12 Employment Relations Act, ss 123(1)(b) and 128. 13 Employment Relations Act, ss 123(1)(c). (d) $1,275.00 ( gross) for public holiday pay. [62] There is no counterclaim before the Authority in relation to the alleged money owing to ABS by Mr Isaako for remedial work, as such no offset can or should be made. Costs [63] As ABS was not represented and did not participate in proceedings, it is not appropriate to reserve costs in the circumstances. [64] Mr Isaako is entitled to a contribution to his costs as he has been successful. When considering costs, the starting point is the Authority’s daily tariff, which is $4,500 for a one-day investigation meeting. The investigation meeting was completed in half a day. [65] ABS did not actively engage with proceedings did not appear at the investigation meeting. In the circumstances it is appropriate to award $2,250 in costs. [66] Accordingly, within 28 days of the date of this determination ABS Builders Limited is ordered to pay Lautusi Isaako $2,250 in costs and reimburse the application of fee of $71.55 Andrew Gane Member of the Employment Relations Authority

[61] Mr Lin told the Authority that NZNIL’s assumption at that point was that Mr Lu had remained in China and not come to New Zealand. He wanted to check that Mr Lu was legitimately wanting work, after not reporting in for some months after his visa was granted. [62] On about 17 November Mr Lu went to the company’s address on the employment agreement. The salesperson gave Mr Lu the number for Mr Lin and in response to a question from Mr Lu, indicated he did not think they needed staff. [63] Mr Lu called Mr Lin. There is a voice recording of this call which has been transcribed and interpreted. Mr Lu introduced himself as having a work visa with the business and coming in June (to Auckland or New Zealand presumably). He felt Mr Lin was unaware of Mr Lu coming. Mr Lin said that the agent did not inform him and asked why Mr Lu did not make contact. Mr Lu replied that he did not have “your way”, possibly ‘a way to contact’ but he told the agent he had come. [64] Mr Lin said he will make a note of Mr Lu’s information – asking for his name, phone number, where he lives. Further he would check with the agency and will be in touch. Mr Lu talked of paying so much money to get here and still there being no job. Mr Lin said he will ask and reply in a day or two, with Mr Lu having his contact number. Mr Lu repeatedly mentioned he has been here a long time and does not want to wait. [65] On 20 November 2023 a text message was sent to Mr Lu in Mandarin – “Hello, please email your situation to our HR department’s email address buyanzrm…. And they will assist in handling it. Thank you”. [66] Mr Lu was suspicious and did not respond. [67] Another email was sent on 25 November at 1.43am in the morning from the bayanz address with the subject line “Employee Entry Application Form”: Please fill it out, sign and send it back and then we will provide you with the induction training. [68] An employee recruitment application form is attached – requiring personal information, including detailed educational background, work experience, reason for the application. This asked the writer to “briefly explain why you are interested in the position and why you believe you are suitable for the role”. [69] Mr Lu described thinking the emails were a scam, having no signature, no name, no job title. Mr Lu did not think this was how a normal company would operate, in such a hostile way, not identifying where the employee was expected to go, telling him if he did not turn up shortly he would be fired. He found the approach very unusual seeing it as a scam in light of Mr Z’s statements that there was no job. He felt like the company was trying to brush him off. He was already formally an employee and it was not necessary for him to reapply for his job. [70] Mr Lin described all this as part of the on-boarding process. He told the Authority that the email address used was not the one he used but thought it was used by the HR assistant and provided her first name. He told the Authority he thought he had instructed her to send both emails but was unable to provide any explanation as to why she might have been sending them late at night. An employee of that name was identified from the payroll information NZNIL provided but showed payments until February 2023 then nothing until April 2024. No alternative explanation was provided. [71] Mr Lu found the two emails very hostile and did not think a company acting in good faith would operate like that. He was affected by his previous experience with Mr Z, sensing that he had been scammed regarding previous jobs. He felt that if he went in to work his employer would find some reason to fire him, especially after the reference to dismissal (or termination) in the first email. [72] On 28 November 2023 Mr Lu went back to China. The same day Mr Lu’s advocate wrote to NZNIL raising claims including migrant exploitation and unjustifiable disadvantage. NZNIL instructed an HR advisory business to represent it. [73] At points after that, including at the investigation meeting, Mr Lin on behalf of NZNIL offered Mr Lu the opportunity to come and work for the company. Mr Lu did not take up this offer, noting that he left for China the same day his advocate raised his concerns. Conclusions [74] Mr Lu arrived in New Zealand on 27 June 2023, leaving again on 18 July. He returned again on 17 October, with his final departure being on 28 November 2023. This is perhaps an unusual pattern. [75] Submissions on behalf of NZNIL portray a picture of Mr Lu seeking to secure employment in the landscaping industry on his arrival in New Zealand and his pursuit of a personal grievance only following the breakdown of his relationship with Mr Z, after Mr Z was unable to provide any employment for Mr Lu. Mr Lu was capable of making online job applications in New Zealand in mid-2023. [76] However, even if Mr Lu was not focused on his arrival on seeking to start with NZNIL, the company was not worried about when he started, making no effort to get a start date, or otherwise follow up with Mr Liu until November. This was despite Mr Lin indicating it was expecting Mr Lu to arrive in about September 2023. The number employed by NZNIL in relation to the size of the premises is hard to easily rationalise. [77] Neither party made the types of attempts one might have expected to get hold of each other reasonably promptly. [78] When Mr Lu did eventually contact the company he did not get a particularly warm welcome. Mr Lin seemed uncertain who he was and wanted to check with the licenced immigration advisor. [79] There are elements in the evidence about both parties suggesting neither may have had the usual intentions in entering into an employment relationship. However, in the absence of more definitive evidence I am reluctant to find that either operated on a false basis and thus assume that they both intended for Mr Lu to work at NZNIL Premium [80] It appears Mr Lu paid a large amount of money in order to obtain the job offer and immigration assistance. The difficulty is, that was not satisfactorily established to be at the demand of Mr Lin and NZNIL. Under s 12A of the Wages Protection Act 1983 no employer or anyone engaged on behalf of it may seek or receive a premium in respect of the employment of any person. [81] The difficulty here is that there has been no connection established between NZNIL or Mr Lin and Mr Z. Mr Lin had contact with Mr Liu who had contact with Mr Z but Mr Lin and Mr Liu’s firm had what appears to be a proper engagement agreement and NZNIL made documented payments to Mr Liu’s company for work undertaken. No evidence establishes what happened to Mr Lu’s money after it went to Mr Z. [82] Recovery of premium money from NZNIL under s 12A(2) of the Wages Protection Act does not come into play as I cannot say that the company or Mr Lin received premium money. Unpaid wages or disadvantage on payment [83] As Mr Lu was back in China for three months and did not attempt to contact NZNIL until November 2023 he cannot establish that he was ready, willing and able to work before that point. NZNIL did not unjustifiably disadvantage him by failing to offer him work or pay him until he contacted the company. Likewise he has no claim to arrears of wages. Dismissal [84] The grievance letter refers to unjustifiable disadvantage rather than dismissal although this was written on the day of Mr Lu’s departure from New Zealand. The statement of problem refers to a disadvantage grievance regarding not providing the contractual working hours and constructive dismissal. Constructive dismissal [85] Constructive dismissal covers situations where although the employee resigns the impetus for the termination comes from the employer. Of the three categories of constructive dismissal described by the Court of Appeal in Auckland Shop Employees Union v Woolworths (NZ) Limited the second two are potentially applicable here: • the employer followed a course of conduct with the deliberate and dominant purpose of coercing the employee to resign; and • a breach of duty by the employer leading the employee to resign.2 [86] A course of conduct with the deliberate and dominant purpose of coercing Mr Lu to resign was not evident. Mr Lin expressed an on-going willingness to have Mr Lu return to work, even with some impracticality. [87] For the third category it is not sufficient for the employer’s conduct to be inconsiderate and cause some unhappiness to the employee.3 What is required is dismissive or repudiatory conduct - a breach of the employer’s duty to the employee. If that is established, these factors need to be examined: • whether the conduct caused the resignation; and 2 Auckland Shop Employees Union v Woolworths (NZ) Limited [1985] 2 NZLR 372 (CA) at 374-375. 3 Wellington etc Clerical Workers etc IUOW v Greenwich (1983) ERNZ Sel Cas 95 (AC). • the breach of duty was sufficiently serious to make it reasonably foreseeable by the employer that the employee would not be prepared to work under the conditions prevailing? Or, was there a substantial risk of resignation? 4 [88] The grievance letter refers to the employer’s objective of getting rid of the employee, although this includes reference to no contact being attempted by the employer for five months, when the same could be said of the employee. [89] NZNIL describes trying to get Mr Lu to report to the office for induction. Mr Lin referred to workers usually contacting the company after they landed on flights from overseas, filling in the recruitment form, then there is a briefing where they can identify what the company can do. [90] Mr Lin’s response to the proposition that the emails looked like a scam, including because late at night, was to suggest that if Mr Lu was in doubt he could have called him. [91] It is hard to see that any breaches of a notional duty to be sufficiently welcoming over a few days would make it foreseeable that an employee would decide to give up and immediately depart for their homeland. Mr Lu was no doubt feeling aggrieved at Mr Z’s failure to provide him the landscape design job Mr Z had promised and Mr Lu had paid for. But given that has not been established to be a breach of duty by NZNIL, so cannot be added into the foreseeability mix. [92] More anticipated responses to a cool welcome might have been to phone Mr Lin and check what was going on, email back querying the form as he already had an employment agreement or fill out the form and hope for the best. [93] Mr Lu’s departure was not foreseeable at that point and he has not established that he was constructively dismissed. Disadvantage grievance [94] The Authority has the power to find a different type of grievance to that alleged.5 I conclude that although Mr Lu was not unjustifiably dismissed he was disadvantaged 4 Auckland Electric Power Board v Auckland Provincial District Local Authorities Officers IUOW [1994] NZLR 415 (CA). 5 The Act, ss 122 and 160(3) by the unjustifiable action of NZNIL in treating him like he was a job applicant rather than someone with an employment agreement with the company. [95] Considering s 103A(5) of the Act, this is not a minor matter resulting in no to Mr Lu. [96] Lost wages are not appropriate as this is not a dismissal grievance and Mr Lu cut off his possibility of having work with NZNIL by leaving the country so promptly. [97] Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act is appropriate. I have set aside the impact on Mr Lu of having paid for a job and the difficulties with Mr Z. Still, having made contact with the employer identified in his employment agreement, Mr Lu as a person intending to work was treated in an unusual and cursory manner – checks being required, receiving late night emails and texts without identification of who they were from and being asked to fill at a recruitment form that strongly suggested he was seeking an appointment and not already covered by an employment agreement.6 [98] Mr Lu was already under stress but this was significantly added to by NZNIL’s approach. It was undignified to be treated as an applicant applying for a job when he had already been offered and accepted one. Mr Lu’s feelings were hurt that his employer was not adopting a welcoming approach for no known reason. [99] Mr Lu is entitled to compensation. I do not conclude that he was blameworthy as regards the way he was treated once he approached NZNIL and it is understandable that he was reluctant to subsequently take up the NZNIL job once he had returned to his family in China. So no deduction for any contribution is warranted. [100] Within 28 days of the date of this determination NZNIL is to pay Mr Lu $15,000 as compensation for the impact on him of his disadvantage grievance. Costs [101] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. 6 The Act, s 5. [102] If they are not able to reach an agreement on costs then if Mr Lu seeks to pursue the matter he should lodge and serve a costs memorandum within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum NZNIL would then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. [103] The Authority’s usual notional daily tariff and any factors requiring an upward or downward adjustment would be considered.7 The starting point is $4,500 for the first day and $3,500 for each full subsequent day, before any increases or decreases are made. Nicola Craig Member of the Employment Relations Authority 7 See www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies.

order_excerpt: applicant did not receive paid breaks from FFDL, and FFDL did not pay each applicant their correct holiday and leave entitlements. (c) Each applicant is owed wage arrears in the amount calculated by them and as presented in their wage calculation spreadsheet. Mr S Prasad is owed $85,918.52, Nishal Lal is owed $136,802.31, Mr Verma is owed $161,552.59 and Mr M Prasad is owed $72,090.93. Unlawful premium [21] Pursuant to s 12A Wages Protection Act 1983, no employer may seek or receive a premium for employment from any person employed by it (or proposed to be employed by it) and if this occurs then the employee may recover the amount paid, as a premium, through the Authority. [22] Mr Verma says that when he was offered employment by FFDL he was told he would need to pay $15,000 for the job and to assist with obtaining residency for him; he subsequently paid $8,000 to Mr Ali as part payment - Mr Verma produced evidence of the bank transfer of $8,000 to Mr Ali. [23] Mr Ali says FFDL did not ask for any money from Mr Verma for his employment rather the $8,000 payment was a loan made by Mr Verma that had been repaid. [24] I am satisfied that Mr Verma paid $8,000 to FFDL for his employment. This payment was an unlawful premium and Mr Verma is entitled to be repaid $8,000 from FFDL. Unjustifiable action causing disadvantage Issues [25] A personal grievance for unjustifiable action causing disadvantage to an employee’s employment is set out in s 103(1)(b) of the Act. This states that an employee may have a personal grievance where the employee’s employment or any condition of employment is or was affected to the employee’s disadvantage by some unjustifiable action by their employer. [26] The applicants allege that FFDL made them work long hours without paying them correctly, without providing rest breaks and without giving each of them their proper leave entitlements. They say these actions by FFDL caused a disadvantage to their employment and the actions by FFDL were not justified. Analysis – did FFDL act as alleged? [27] I have already determined that FFDL required the applicants to work at least 60 hours per week and then failed to pay the applicants for all the hours they worked, failed to provide the applicants with rest breaks and did not give the applicants their proper leave entitlements. Analysis - did FFDL’s actions cause a disadvantage to the applicants’ employment? [28] These actions by FFDL caused a disadvantage to each applicant’s employment. Analysis – were FFDL’s actions justified? [29] These actions by FFDL were not justified – they were not the actions that a fair and reasonable employer could have undertaken in the circumstances as FFDL failed to meet minimum employment standards for each applicant. [30] Conclusion on the applicants’ personal grievances for unjustifiable action causing disadvantage [31] Each applicant has established a personal grievance for unjustifiable actions by FFDL that caused a disadvantage to their employment. Unjustifiable dismissal Issues [32] The issues for an unjustifiable dismissal grievance are: (a) Was the employee dismissed; and (a) If so, were the actions of the employer in deciding to dismiss the employee, justifiable? What happened? [33] In September 2021 FFDL completed the sale of Krazy Price Mart. As a result, each applicant’s employment with FFDL was terminated. The applicants were offered and took up new employment with the purchasers of Krazy Price Mart. [34] The applicants say their dismissals were not justified as they were not consulted over the possible sale of Krazy Price Mart. FFDL says it did consult with the applicants over the sale of Krazy Price Mart; it refers to three meetings in which discussions took place, with one of them being a farewell dinner for the applicants. The applicants were dismissed [35] In this case all four applicants were dismissed by FFDL on 1 September 2021 when Krazy Price Mart was sold. Were FFDL’s actions in dismissing the applicants justified? [36] The test for justification is set out in s 103A of the Act; the test being whether the actions of the employer were what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances. Applying that test here the question is whether FFDL’s actions in reaching the decision to dismiss the applicants were the actions a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances at the time – this applies to the process adopted by FFDL and the substantive justification for the decision. [37] In terms of process, a fair process is governed by s 4(1A) and s 103A of the Act. In this case a fair process involves FFDL consulting with the applicants over the potential sale of Krazy Price Mart and giving them an opportunity to provide feedback on the potential loss of their employment. [38] Having considered the evidence of the applicants and Mr Ali I find that FFDL did not consult adequately with the applicants over the sale of Krazy Price Mart store; there was no substantive consultation and no opportunity for the applicants to provide feedback over the potential loss of their employment. [39] Each applicant was unjustifiable dismissed by FFDL. Remedies for the applicants’ personal grievances [40] As each applicant has been successful with two personal grievances, I must turn to consider what remedies they may be entitled to. In this regard, I may award any of the remedies provided for under s 123 of the Act. The remedies sought by each applicant [41] Each applicant seeks: (a) Compensation - this is an award for the humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings that an applicant suffers from the unjustified actions of the employer and the award is made pursuant to s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act. (b) Lost remuneration – if an applicant has lost remuneration because of their personal grievances then pursuant to sections 123 and 128 of the Act, I may reimburse them for their lost remuneration. In this case I am not satisfied that the applicants lost remuneration as a result of their unjustifiable dismissal. [42] So, I find the applicants are entitled to compensation for their personal grievances but not lost remuneration. [43] I will turn to consider the level of compensation for each applicant. My task is to quantify the harm and loss caused by the humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings arising out of the dismissals and unjustified actions by FFDL. Recent decisions of the Employment Court provide guidance on this exercise of quantification.2 Compensation [44] Each applicant gave evidence of the impact of FFDL’s unjustified actions on them. All four applicants suffered from working extensively without being paid correctly. The applicants described themselves as being exploited and being treated like slaves. This treatment impacted their mental and physical health, particularly manifesting in loss of self-esteem, loss of confidence and self-worth and physical symptoms such as headaches and feeling tired and exhausted. They all spoke of humiliation, shame and embarrassment as to how they were treated and they spoke about suffering from stress, anxiety, pain and suffering, such as sleeplessness 2 Stormont v Peddle Thorp Aitken Ltd [2017] NZEmpC 71, Waikato District Health Board v Kathleen Ann Archibald [2017] NZEmpC 132, Richora Group Ltd v Cheng [2018] NZEmpC 113. and mental torture. Significantly, they all suffered extreme financial pressure which disrupted their day-to-day life. [45] All this harm and loss was then compounded by the applicants’ unjustified dismissal. [46] I am satisfied that for each of the applicants the quantum for the harm and loss suffered should be $32,000.00. Contribution [47] As I have awarded compensation to the applicants, I must now consider whether they contributed to the situation that gave rise to their grievances.3 This assessment requires me to determine if they behaved in a manner that was culpable or blameworthy, and this behaviour contributed to their grievances.4 [48] Having assessed the evidence I conclude that none of the applicants acted in a manner that contributed to their grievances such that the compensation I have awarded should be reduced. Persons involved in the breaches [49] The applicants seek orders against Mr and Mrs Ali as persons involved in breaches of employment standards pursuant to ss 142W and 142Y of the Act. [50] Having assessed the evidence I am satisfied that: (a) Mr Ali was involved in the day-to-day management of Krazy Price Mart and made many of the decisions about the work the applicants did and the payment they received. Mr Ali is clearly a person involved in the breaches of employment standards by FFDL. (b) Mrs Ali was not involved in the day-to-day management of Krazy Price Mart and did not make, nor was she involved in, the decisions relating to the applicants’ work and pay. Mrs Ali is not a person involved in breaches of employment standards by FFDL. 3 Section 124 of the Act. 4 Xtreme Dining Ltd v Dewar [2016] NZEmpC 136 [51] As a result of my order against Mr Ali, if FFDL does not pay the wage arrears owed to the applicants they can apply to Authority for an order that Mr Ali pay. [52] I can also award penalties against Mr Ali – I will address this below. Piercing the corporate veil [53] The applicants seek to have me pierce the corporate veil so that Mr and Mrs Ali are deemed to be personally liable for the compensation orders I have made. [54] This is not an issue I will address now. This is a matter of enforcement of the orders made against FFDL and can be considered later – at this point I raise concerns I have about whether such enforcement is an employment relationship problem and is within the Authority’s jurisdiction and if it is whether the grounds are made out for the orders sought. Penalties [55] The applicants seek penalties against FFDL and Mr Ali as a person involved in the breaches of employment standards. [56] In respect of any penalties against Mr Ali I do not appear to have evidence before me that penalties were sought from him within 12 months of the relevant events – so I cannot order any penalties at present.5 [57] In respect of penalties against FFDL I am satisfied that I can consider penalties against it for the following breaches (based on what has been sought by the applicants and the breaches by FFDL that I have determined occurred): (a) Four breaches of good faith. (b) One breach of the Wages Protection Act 1983 for the premium paid for Mr Verma’s employment. (c) Four global breaches of Holidays Act 2003 – that is one global for each applicant covering FFDL’s failure to properly provide the applicants with annual leave entitlements, deal with the applicants working on public holidays correctly and provide the applicants with sick leave. 5 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 135(5). [58] If the applicants wish to pursue penalties against FFDL and Mr Ali then they can lodge submissions on quantum and payment of penalties, and in the case of Mr Ali provide information regarding when an action for the recovery of penalties from him was first commenced. These submissions are to be lodged and served with 28 days of this determination. FFDL and/or Mr Ali will then have 14 days to lodge and serve any submissions in reply. Summary and orders [59] FFDL did not pay the four applicants correctly for the hours they worked, and it did not calculate their holiday and leave entitlements correctly. [60] FFDL acted in an unjustified manner toward each applicant causing disadvantage to their employment by requiring them to work excessive hours and not paying them correctly. [61] FFDL unjustifiably dismissed each applicant. [62] In settlement of the personal grievances and wage arrears claim Fiji Food Distributors NZ Limited must pay: (a) $85,918.52 in wage arrears to Mr S Prasad. (b) $136,802.31 in wage arrears to Mr Lal. (c) $161,552.59 in wage arrears to Mr Verma. (d) $72,090.93 in wage arrears to Mr M Prasad. (e) $8,000 for an unlawful premium to Mr Verma. (f) $32,000.00 to each applicant for compensation pursuant to s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Employment Relations Act 2000. Costs [63] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. [64] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, the applicants may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum Fiji Food Distributors NZ Limited will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [65] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.6 Peter van Keulen Member of the Employment Relations Authority 6 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

order_excerpt: Remedies Reimbursement of lost wages [37] Mr Byrne seeks reimbursement of earnings lost as a result of his dismissal pursuant to section 123(1)(b) and 128 of the Act. The period of claim is from 14 March 2025, when Mr Byrne’s notice period expired to date of determination and for a further six months from that date. [38] Mr Byrne says the job market is very challenging, his age is a significant factor against him and these were factors known to or could reasonably have been known to RDL when it dismissed him. RDL submits it has empathy for Mr Byrne’s situation, but it was inevitable there would be job losses with the restructuring of the Hamer business unit, reasonable efforts were taken to maintain the employment relationship and it cannot be held responsible for Mr Byrne’s financial circumstances or the lack of success he has had to date in finding another job. [39] After reviewing the evidence of loss and Mr Byrne’s attempts to mitigate that loss the Authority is satisfied he is entitled to an award of three-months ordinary pay. Eight per-cent holiday pay and the 3% Kiwisaver contribution are to be calculated and paid on the three-month award. I decline to exercise my discretion and award more than the three-month ordinary time remuneration. The evidence indicates Mr Byrne can look for other work and though it is accepted the labour market is challenging this is a factor outside the scope of the found personal grievance. Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings [40] Mr Byrne said his dismissal has had a severe impact on his overall well-being and undermined his confidence. He said he remains unclear why he was selected for redundancy and feels strongly that matters undisclosed and unfairly prejudicial to him motivated RDL’s actions. With the support of RDL he accessed counselling services and the evidence before the Authority is this was a positive step. Jack Byrne said his father is a good man and losing his job has hit him hard. [41] It is accepted the impact of his personal grievance has had a negative impact on Mr Byrne. The Authority is satisfied he has experienced harm under each of the heads in section 123(1)(c)(i). Having regard to the particular circumstances of this matter Mr Byrne is entitled to an award to compensate the humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings he has suffered consequent to he established personal grievance of $16,000.00. Reimbursement of lost benefits [42] The parties’ employment agreement provided Mr Byrne had use of the company vehicle for business purposes.13 Notwithstanding, with the full knowledge of RDL he used the vehicle to travel to and from work from his home and had use of the company fuel card to pay for petrol used for this purpose at the rate of $150 per week including GST. This is a benefit he enjoyed during his employment, and he is entitled to be reimbursed for it for 3 months at a rate of $150 per week less GST. 13 Individual employment agreement, schedule 3, clause 6. If any remedy is awarded, should it be reduced (under s 124 of the Act) for blameworthy conduct by Mr Byrne that contributed to the situation giving rise to his grievance? [43] No deduction from the remedies awarded is to be made under s 124 of the Act. Mr Byrne’s dismissal was a no-fault redundancy and he did not contribute in a blameworthy way to the situation giving rise to his personal grievance. Penalty [44] Mr Byrne seeks a penalty for actions of RDL’s which he says were not consistent with the section 4 duty of good faith. I have found RDL’s failure to provide Mr Byrne with the information it sought and received about the recordings was a breach of this duty and the failure to consult with him about the redeployment opportunity was a breach of the parties’ employment agreement. Mr Byrne has claimed the later breach as a breach of the duty of good faith. There are a range of other matters which he points to as breaches of good faith. My view is these other matters are of such a type that they are and have been properly folded in the consideration of his personal grievance and the remedies awarded. [45] The maximum penalty against a company is $20,000.14 In considering whether a penalty is warranted and, if so, at what level, regard is had to the factors set out in s 133A of the Act, as well as the Employment Court decisions in Nicholson v Ford and A Labour Inspector v Daleson Investment Ltd.15 [46] I am satisfied RDL failed in its duty of good faith to Mr Byrne to disclose the information about the secret recording and to consult with him on the deployment options, if any. These are failures to actively and constructively engage with Mr Byrne about matters directly relevant to the maintenance of a productive employment relationship. The matters were relevant and acute to the employment environment because Mr Byrne was a directly affected employee under the restructuring proposal. In addition, these were matters entirely within RDL’s control which have had a significant and negative impact on Mr Byrne. 14 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 135. 15 Nicholson v Ford [2018] NZEmpC 132 and Labour Inspector v Daleson Investment Ltd [2019]. [47] Applying the relevant considerations in a penalty setting a penalty of $1000 is warranted to be paid within 21 days of today’s date half of which is to be paid to Mr Byrne. Summary of orders [48] Within 21 days of the date of determination Rushmore Distributors (NZ) Limited is to make the following payments to Andrew Byrne: a) lost wages under s 123(1)(b) of the Act in an amount equivalent to 3 months ordinary time remuneration plus eight per-cent holiday pay and the employer Kiwisaver contribution; b) compensation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act in the amount of $16,000 for the personal grievance; c) compensation under s 123(1)(c)(ii) of the Act in the gross amount of $150 per week less GST for 3 months to reimburse the established lost benefit; and d) a penalty of $1000, half to be paid to the Crown and half to Mr Byrne. Costs [49] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, Mr Byrne may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 14 days of the date of this determination.
